title: Can a thin zigzag have a longer boundary than a square?
description: A four by four square is set beside a thin zigzag of nine unit squares joined edge to edge. The boundary is counted for each shape and then the unit squares inside. Keeko doubts this and says the zigzag covers more because its boundary winds so far.
teaching_notes: One idea: count the boundary edges for the perimeter and the squares for the area, and the two need not agree. Watch for children who think a long winding boundary means a large area.

source: Compare a 4 by 4 square with a thin zigzag made of 9 unit sq
video_script.why: The child meets two regions of other shapes where the one with the larger perimeter has the smaller area, as the book asks.
video_script.substitution: Count the boundary edges and the unit squares of the square and of the zigzag, then compare.
video_script.anchor: a four by four square and a thin zigzag of nine unit squares, the two regions of other shapes that the book asks for
video_script.wrong_answer: the zigzag covers more because its boundary is longer
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko reads the long winding boundary as a large area. Counting the squares gives the zigzag 9 and the square 16.
video_script.payoff_line: the zigzag has the larger perimeter but the smaller area

final_answer.value: The zigzag has the larger perimeter (20 units against 16) but the smaller area (9 against 16)
final_answer.spoken: twenty units against sixteen, and nine square units against sixteen

hold_back: the zigzag has the larger perimeter but the smaller area
never_show: which shape has the larger perimeter or area, before the compare step
maths_rules: square 4 by 4: perimeter 4 × 4 = 16 units; area 4 × 4 = 16 square units
zigzag of 9 unit squares in one line with bends, only neighbours touching: 8 joins
zigzag boundary: 9 × 4 = 36 edges in all, 8 joins hide 2 edges each = 16, so 36 − 16 = 20 units
zigzag area: 9 unit squares = 9 square units
video_script.design: One idea: boundary edges give the perimeter, squares give the area. Wrong idea: a long boundary means a large area. The square and the zigzag stay on stage from the hook to the end. The zigzag is a staircase, so only neighbours in the line touch.
open_questions: The book has no picture of the zigzag; the video draws it as a staircase of nine unit squares, which the worklist example describes.

<bookmark mark='unit'/>A square with every side one unit long is called a unit square.

<bookmark mark='zig'/>Beside it is a thin zigzag of nine unit squares joined edge to edge.
<bookmark mark='peri'/>The length of the boundary of a shape is called its perimeter.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which shape has the longer perimeter, and which one covers more space?

narration: <bookmark mark='peri'/>Step one, the square. Its perimeter is four sides of four units, so four times four gives sixteen units.
<bookmark mark='area'/>Its area is four times four, which is sixteen square units.

beats.on_screen: Zigzag: edges in all = 9 × 4 = 36. Joins: 8, each hides 2 edges, 8 × 2 = 16. Perimeter = 36 − 16 = 20 units

narration: <bookmark mark='all'/>Step two, the zigzag. Nine squares have nine times four, which is thirty six edges in all.
<bookmark mark='joins'/>Eight joins hide two edges each, which is sixteen edges.
<bookmark mark='peri'/>Take sixteen away from thirty six to get a perimeter of twenty units.

beats.on_screen: Answer: the zigzag has the larger perimeter (20 units against 16) but the smaller area (9 against 16)

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The zigzag has the larger perimeter but the smaller area.
Its perimeter is twenty units against sixteen, and its area is nine square units against sixteen.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the zigzag covers more because its boundary is longer.
<bookmark mark='count'/>A winding boundary feels big, but we must count what lies inside. The zigzag holds nine squares and the square holds sixteen.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The boundary and the space inside are two different measures, and they need not agree.
